questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most accurate way to think about AI security relative to the security disciplines you already practice?
options: AI security requires abandoning API security, data classification, and access control entirely and starting over
AI security is mostly an extension of disciplines you already have, applied to a new surface, plus a focused set of genuinely new concerns layered on top
AI security has nothing in common with any traditional security discipline
AI security only applies to companies that train their own foundation models from scratch
questions.explain: The chapter's throughline: the fundamental practice stays the discipline you already know (API security, data classification, supply chain, access control), and the new work is scoping each one to cover the AI-specific surface it now touches.

questions.q: An LLM feature is, underneath, an API call to a model provider or inference endpoint. What does this lesson say still applies in full, and what's new about the payload?
options: Authentication, authorization, rate-limiting, and logging all still apply in full; what's new is that the prompt and response need the extra scrutiny of Prompt Injection and Insecure Output Handling risk
Nothing about traditional API security applies once an LLM is involved
Rate-limiting becomes unnecessary because LLM APIs are never abused
Authentication is optional for LLM APIs since the model itself verifies the caller's identity
questions.explain: The API security fundamentals are unchanged — you're applying them to a payload (the prompt and the model's response) that now carries the Prompt Injection and Insecure Output Handling risks covered earlier in the chapter.

questions.q: Why does data classification now need to extend to training data and retrieval-augmented context, according to this lesson?
options: Because training data is never sensitive and doesn't need classification
Because classification rules only ever applied to databases, never to files
Because sensitive data baked into training risks resurfacing through model memorization, and a retrieval step that isn't access-controlled can pull data the requester isn't authorized to see
Because retrieval-augmented systems are always exempt from data classification policy
questions.explain: If regulated or classified data ends up in training data it can resurface via model memorization (Sensitive Information Disclosure), and an unscoped retrieval step can bypass access control that's enforced everywhere else in the organization.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the relationship between traditional supply chain security and the AI-specific supply chain (foundation models, checkpoints, datasets, plugins)?
options: AI supply chain risk is a brand-new problem with no analogue in traditional security practice
Plugins and datasets pulled from public hubs carry no provenance risk worth tracking

The practice is the same one already used for open-source dependencies — know what you're pulling in, verify its source, track it for known issues — just applied to a parallel AI-specific supply chain
Supply chain security only applies to compiled binaries, not to models or datasets
questions.explain: OWASP's Supply Chain Vulnerabilities category and NIST's Map function both point at the exact discipline already used for open-source dependencies, extended to foundation models, checkpoints, datasets, and plugins.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say least-privilege access control becomes more important, not less, for agentic AI systems?
options: Because agents never need any permissions at all to function
Because access control theory has to be completely reinvented for AI and bears no resemblance to service-account scoping
Because least privilege only matters for human users, never for automated service accounts or agents
Because an over-permissioned agent executing a manipulated model's request as a real action is exactly what turns a successful prompt injection into Excessive Agency harm
questions.explain: The model being manipulated is the attack; an agent holding more permission than its task needs is what lets that manipulation cascade into a real, consequential action — exactly the Excessive Agency risk from Lesson 2.
